query: For high-entropy alloys intended as intermediate materials in plasma-facing reactor components, what single intervention could improve heat-transfer capability while preserving structural integrity? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the expected outcome compared with current intermediate-layer performance, the temperature and loading conditions under which it should hold, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The introduction of a high-entropy alloy (HEA) interlayer with optimized lattice misfit between the tungsten plasma-facing material and the CuCrZr alloy heat sink can improve heat-transfer capability while preserving structural integrity in plasma-facing reactor components.
generation.material_initial_state: Tungsten plasma-facing material and CuCrZr alloy heat sink
generation.intervention: Introduction of a high-entropy alloy (HEA) interlayer
generation.structural_mediator: Optimized lattice misfit between the HEA interlayer and the tungsten plasma-facing material
generation.mechanism: Enhanced interface stability and improved thermal conductivity due to the optimized lattice misfit
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved heat-transfer capability and preserved structural integrity
generation.baseline: Current intermediate-layer performance using traditional materials
generation.boundary: Temperature range: 180-350 °C, neutron irradiation: up to 150 dpa
generation.uncertainty: The exact composition and lattice misfit of the HEA interlayer required for optimal performance are uncertain

falsification_experiment.design: Comparative study of heat-transfer capability and structural integrity of plasma-facing reactor components with and without the HEA interlayer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA interlayer does not improve heat-transfer capability or preserve structural integrity, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: The development of advanced materials capable of withstanding the extreme conditions in nuclear fusion reactors represents a critical challenge for achieving sustainable fusion energy,. Plasma-facing materials (PFMs), which are directly exposed to intense particle fluxes and extreme heat from high-temperature plasma, must simultaneously resist high-energy neutron irradiation and withstand helium (He) and hydrogen (H) fluxes from the plasma environment. Tungsten (W) has been recognized as a leading plasma-facing material due to its remarkable properties. Its refractory nature, high melting point, excellent thermal conductivity, low erosion rates, and outstanding thermomechanical stability make it highly suitable for use as the first wall material in ITER and future fusion reactors. However, the formation of helium (He) bubbles during helium irradiation raises significant concerns about the long-term structural integrity of plasma-facing components manufactured from pure tungsten,. In recent years, high-entropy alloys (HEAs) have been identified as promising alternatives to traditional materials for use in extreme environments. cited_evidence.kind: web:3.4. Effect of γ/γ′ Lattice Misfit on the Creep Properties of HESA
cited_evidence.text: On the whole, the influence of γ/γ′ lattice misfit on the creep behavior of HESAs parallels has been observed in conventional Ni-based superalloys. Alloys with a negative lattice misfit consistently demonstrate superior creep performance due to enhanced interface stability. When the lattice misfit is small, creep resistance improves with increasing |δ|. However, beyond an optimal range, excessive misfit impairs phase stability, thereby accelerating creep. Therefore, optimizing the lattice misfit—ensuring it remains negative and within a moderate range—is essential for improving the creep resistance and structural integrity of HESAs under high-temperature service conditions.
